headline: After a sharply colder, sunny Tuesday and Wednesday, a strong storm on Thanksgiving will likely bring 1–2 inches of rain, east-northeast gusts of 35–45 mph (possibly over 50 mph at the coast) and widespread, possibly locally major, coastal flooding.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A cold front moved through Monday afternoon, ending a run of unusually mild afternoons and bringing in much colder air. Winds ease Monday evening, though New York City and the nearby airports can still see gusts around 17–23 mph much of the night under dry skies. For reference, Monday's record highs are 72 at Central Park and 74 at Newark (both 1931), and 70 at LaGuardia and 71 at JFK (both 1992).

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Tuesday is sunny but much colder, with highs struggling to reach 50 and most places topping out in the upper 40s; northwest winds gust around 17–29 mph from late morning into the afternoon before easing in the evening. Tuesday night is the coldest night of the season so far, dropping below freezing outside the New York City metro area and into the mid 30s in the city itself. Wednesday is similar, with winds turning northeast and clouds increasing in the afternoon ahead of a storm approaching from the south.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: An impactful storm is increasingly likely on Thanksgiving, as a very strong high over the Northeast squeezes against a deepening low moving up into the Mid-Atlantic: east-northeast winds of 15–25 mph develop by late Thursday morning, with gusts peaking at 35–45 mph Thursday afternoon and evening, possibly over 50 mph along the coast for a time, and wind advisories may eventually be needed. A period of steady moderate, locally heavy rain arrives Thursday into Thursday night, starting as early as Thursday morning or as late as early Thursday evening because the main computer models still differ by 6–12 hours; 1–2 inches is expected on average, with localized amounts near 3 inches. A low-end (marginal) risk of excessive rain covers the whole region, but minor flooding in urban and poor-drainage areas is far more likely than flash flooding, and river and stream flooding should be limited because the storm moves through quickly. Friday turns blustery with west winds gusting about 29–40 mph as the storm departs, and Saturday stays breezy with west gusts of about 23–35 mph.

coast: Coastal flooding is growing more likely, with a full moon on Tuesday the 24th and king tides this week: many locations need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding. Localized minor coastal flooding is possible with Wednesday morning's high tide, then the forecast supports widespread minor to moderate flooding from Thursday morning through Friday morning. Localized major flooding is possible in the most vulnerable spots along the South Shore back bays and western Great South Bay, and at a few northeast New Jersey spots such as Kearny Point and the Hackensack River; some guidance (such as the Stevens model) has raised the odds of localized major flooding. How fast and how far inland the storm tracks will decide how long the flood-driving east-northeast winds last before turning south-southwest. Beach flooding, erosion and overwash are all possible, though overwash looks isolated for now. On the water, Small Craft Advisories run until 1 AM Tuesday for Long Island Sound east of the Connecticut River and until 1 PM Tuesday for the nearshore ocean waters, with seas near 5 feet and gusts near 29 mph (25 knots) Tuesday afternoon before conditions ease Tuesday evening. After a lull into Wednesday, winds ramp up Wednesday night: gale-force winds (about 39–54 mph) are likely on all waters, with possible storm-force winds on the ocean Thursday into Thursday evening, and waves up to 15–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound east of Orient Point; gales may continue into Friday.
watch_for: Widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding Thursday morning through Friday morning, possibly major in the most vulnerable spots, helped by king tides and the full moon.
Thanksgiving wind gusts of 35–45 mph, possibly over 50 mph along the coast, strongest Thursday afternoon and evening.
Rain timing on Thanksgiving (morning versus evening) and totals of 1–2 inches, locally near 3.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the sharply colder, dry Monday night through Wednesday and increasingly confident in an impactful Thanksgiving storm, but with the storm still several days out, rain timing, wind strength and how severe the coastal flooding gets still vary among the models.
